food.text: Inca cuisine flourished from the 13th to the 16th century across a huge stretch of western South America. Its most important plant staples were tubers, roots and grains, while the most common meats were guinea pigs, llamas and fish.

The Inca realm ran north to south through many climate zones, and the mountains of Peru offered growing zones at very different altitudes. Terraces built at different heights let the Incas cultivate a wide number of staples.

Corn beer, called chicha de jora, was the most common form of chicha, a drink that emerged from the Andes and Amazonia. In the Inca Empire, chicha had ceremonial and ritual uses, and the Inca consumed it in vast quantities during religious festivals. Human sacrifices first had to be rubbed in the dregs of chicha, then tube-fed with more chicha for days while lying buried alive in tombs.

Quinoa and cañihua, two members of the Chenopodium family, were part of Inca cooking because they could survive the high altitudes of the Andes. Quinoa has since grown popular far beyond the Andes for its adaptability and nutritional value.

Roots and tubers provided the staples of the Inca, yet they were still ranked lower than maize. Ullucu and arracacha, which tastes something like a cross between carrot and celery, were used like potatoes in stews and soups.

Chicha was central to the economy of the Incas, and the place where maize was planted was taken very seriously. Because planting maize showed an important social role, the state would probably have run these farms, and drinking chicha together as a community was part of everyday life. The Incas also saw chicha in a sexual way, as semen, and when they poured it onto the Earth they thought they were feeding the Earth.

Tarwi, also called chocho, is a high-altitude plant rich in protein that the Incas often ate with chilis and onions. It had to be carefully treated first, because improper treatment can leave the crop poisonous.
Achira, a sweet, starchy root, was baked in earth ovens. It had to be transported up to the power center of Cuzco, so it is considered to have been food eaten as part of a tradition.

Several kinds of seaweed, including Porphyra and Ulva lactuca, were part of the Inca diet and could be eaten fresh or dried. Freshwater algae of the genus Nostoc were eaten raw or processed for storage.

The Inca ate animals that many Europeans considered vermin, such as frogs, caterpillars, beetles and ants. Mayfly larvae were eaten raw, or toasted and ground to make loaves that could then be stored.
Pepino, a refreshing and thirst-quenching fruit, was eaten by common folk in Inca cuisine. "Pampered folk" scorned it, and it was considered difficult to digest.

art.text: Between the 9th and 13th centuries CE, the Tiwanaku empire rose by the borders of Lake Titicaca. Centered around a city of the same name in modern-day Bolivia, the Tiwanaku introduced stone architecture and sculpture of a monumental type.

The Chimu were the great city builders of pre-Inca civilization. They were a loose confederation of walled cities scattered along the coast of northern Peru and flourished from about 1140 to 1450. Their capital was at Chan Chan, outside modern-day Trujillo.
The Tiwanaku's monumental stone architecture and sculpture were made possible by their developing bronze. Bronze enabled them to make the tools needed to work the stone.

The Inca Civilization united Peru under its hegemony and incorporated a great part of the cultural legacy of earlier civilizations into its own works. Important relics of Inca art and architecture survive in Cusco, at Sacsahuaman and Machu Picchu, and in stone pavements that united Cusco with the rest of the empire.

Some of Peru's most important buildings stand on the sites of pre-Hispanic constructions in Lima. A temple called Puma Inti once occupied the site of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Lima. The Municipal Theater stands where a structure the Spaniards called Huaca El Cabildo once stood.
The Inca carved artifacts and jewelry from lapis lazuli, a deep-blue stone. The source they used was in the Andes mountains of Chile, where lapis is still extracted near Ovalle.

war.text: According to tradition, in 1438 the Hanan Chanka leader Anccu Hualloc gathered 40,000 warriors and launched the conquest of Cusco. They advanced victoriously and encircled the city, and the Inca Viracocha and many nobles fled toward Qullasuyu in despair. Inca sources describe the Hanan Chankas as bloody in battle, taking prisoners and punishing them cruelly.

Chimor was the last Andean kingdom capable of stopping the Inca Empire. Topa Inca Yupanqui began the Inca conquest in the 1470s and defeated the emperor Minchançaman. It was the largest polity the Inca ever conquered.

Traditional historiography claims that the Inca advance south halted after the Battle of the Maule, where they met determined resistance from the Mapuche. The Inca Empire then reached as far as the north of the Maule River in what is now Chile.

The Inca ruler Tupac Inca Yupanqui conquered the Chachapoyas around 1475, despite fortifications such as the citadel at Kuélap, because their settlements may have become decentralized and fragmented once the threat of Wari invasion had dissipated. The defeat was fairly swift, but smaller rebellions continued for many years. To quell them, the Incas used the mitma system of ethnic dispersion, forcing large numbers of Chachapoya people to resettle in remote locations of the empire. Later, the Chachapoyas were conscripted into Huáscar's army and suffered heavy casualties, and after Atahualpa's victory many more were executed or deported.

With the Chanka besieging Cusco, the prince Cusi Yupanqui bravely led the resistance and offered peace, but the offer was rejected. A bloody battle followed at Yawarpampa, meaning 'field of blood', and Cusco won it with the timely arrival of friendly forces. According to the victors, 22,000 Chancas and 8,000 Cusqueños died there, and Anccu Hualloc was injured and captured.
Before becoming emperor, Topa Inca Yupanqui headed the Inca army on large expeditions to the north. His army besieged and captured Curamba, Huaylla-Pucara, Canta and, most importantly, Chan Chan.
During the 15th century the Inca expanded the fortress of Sacsayhuamán above Cusco, building dry stone walls of huge boulders. Workers cut the stones to fit together tightly without mortar.

Archaeological evidence shows significant interpersonal violence after the Wari state collapsed, suggesting that warfare and raiding increased among rival groups. The city of Wari was dramatically depopulated by 1000 AD after centuries of drought.

The Incas made most of their conquests in the late 15th century, according to both traditional historiography and Silva. Topa Inca Yupanqui reigned from 1471 to 1493, in the traditional dating of that period.

Pachacuti named his son Amaru Yupanqui co-ruler, but Amaru showed little interest in military affairs. After a revolt in which Amaru almost led the Inca forces to defeat, Pachacuti replaced him with another son, Topa Inca Yupanqui.
After defeating Chimor, the Inca moved its final emperor, Minchançaman, to Cusco. They also redirected Chimú gold and silver there to adorn the Qurikancha.

Around 1460, Tupac Inca Yupanqui led an army of 200,000 warriors against the Palta nation. The Cañari resisted fiercely, leaving the Incas so impressed that once defeated, the Cañari were recruited into the Inca army.

In northern Ecuador the Inca army met even fiercer resistance from an alliance between the Quitu and the Cañari. After defeating them in the battle of Atuntaqui, Tupac Yupanqui sent settlers to what is now Quito and left Chalco Mayta as governor.

The Chanka were said to paint their faces and scream when fighting. According to Inca sources, the Hanan Chankas scalped prisoners or skinned them alive. They hung prisoners upside down so the blood gathered in the upper body, made small cuts on the front of the toes and tore the skin off gradually while the prisoner screamed in terror. They also made cups from the skulls of prisoners and drank the enemy's blood from them, earning the nickname "Vampires of the Andes".

literature.text: Before the Spanish arrived, the Andes had no alphabet. Instead, people kept records with quipus, devices made from knotted cords of cotton or camelid fiber. Quipus flourished across the Andes from about 1100 to 1532, and the Inca tied knots in a decimal positional system to store numbers.

Some scholars argue that quipus held far more than numbers and were a true writing system. That would be an especially important discovery, because no written record of the Inca Empire that predates the Spanish invasion survives. The question remains unresolved.

According to Chimú oral history, the story of the kingdom of Chimor began when Taycanamo arrived in the Moche Valley from the sea on a balsa raft. His descendants then conquered the surrounding areas. The Chimú culture arose about 900 CE, and the Inca conquered it around 1470.

Quechua began spreading across the central Andes many centuries before the Incas. The Inca were one of many peoples who already spoke a form of Quechua. The Inca Empire then promoted it as its official language, and the form spoken in the Cuzco region was heavily influenced by Aymara.

Chimú oral history traces the kingdom's growth through Taycanamo's family. His son Guacricur integrated Chimú rule over the lower valley. His grandson Ñancempinco then expanded the kingdom by conquering the upper valley. Ñançenpinco began further expansion both north and south of the Moche Valleys.

Some Quechua poems thought to date from Inca times survive only as quotations inside Spanish-language chronicles about the pre-Conquest period. Like other Andean texts, they were written down in Latin characters after the European conquest. They still express, to a great extent, the culture of pre-Conquest times.

Members of the ruling class were usually taught to read quipus in the yachay wasi, the Inca equivalent of a university. The name means "house of teaching". Reading quipus came in the third year of schooling, for the higher classes who would eventually become the bureaucracy.

Inca historians used quipus when telling the Spanish about the history of Tawantin Suyu. Whether the cords recorded only important numbers or actually contained the story itself is unknown. Quipucamayocs were not the only members of Inca society who used quipus.

According to legend, Taycanamo also founded Chan Chan, the capital of Chimor. Chimor was the last kingdom that had any chance of stopping the Inca Empire. The Inca conquest began in the 1470s under Topa Inca Yupanqui.

Ollantay is a Quechua-language drama that some consider the oldest and deepest expression of Quechua literature. The most widely accepted theory is that its story is of Incan origin and was preserved through oral tradition until it was adapted for the stage in colonial times. Its oldest known manuscript belonged to the priest Antonio Valdés.

science.text: The Incas built one of the greatest imperial states in human history without the wheel, draft animals, or knowledge of iron. Their engineers and farmers instead relied on clever adaptation to the mountains, and the empire grew from the early 13th century highlands around Cusco.

Quipus were record-keeping devices made of knotted cords of cotton or camelid fiber. The Inca used knots tied in a decimal positional system to store numbers and other values, and quipus could have anywhere from a few to several thousand cords.

At Moray, Inca builders made terraced circular depressions, the largest about 30 metres deep. Their depth, design, and orientation to wind and sun create a temperature difference of as much as 15 °C between top and bottom, much like the microclimates of a modern greenhouse.

The Inca road system was about 40,000 kilometres long and was carefully planned, engineered, and maintained. It included paved sections, stairways to gain elevation, bridges, retaining walls, and water drainage systems, all built without the use of wheels.

Inca agriculture had to work in three very different environments: high, cold mountains, a coastal desert that could only be farmed with irrigation, and humid Amazon foothills. Potatoes and quinoa were among the unique Andean crops, and llamas, alpacas and guinea pigs were the domesticated animals.

Inca administration used quipus for monitoring tax obligations, collecting census records, keeping calendrical information, and organizing the military. Quipus flourished across the Andes from about 1100 to 1532, and the Inca kept separate ones for each province.

Machu Picchu's terraces were built by Inca engineers to drain excess water, since the area receives more than 1,800 mm of rain a year. Kenneth Wright's soil analyses in the 1990s showed layers of large stones, gravel, and sand, topped with rich topsoil.

At Tipon, three irrigation canals diverted water from the Rio Pukara to the site's terraces about 1.35 km away. Natural springs there also fed fountains that supplied noble residents with water for non-agricultural purposes.

Soil samples at Moray show that soils were brought in from different regions to help grow crops on the different levels of the terraces. The site is widely believed to have been used for farming, and like many Inca sites it also has an irrigation system.

Along the Inca roads, relay stations housed chasquis, the running messengers. Tambos were placed at one-day walking intervals to support road users and flocks of llamas, helping information move quickly across the empire.

Inca farmers had no domesticated animals suitable for agricultural work, so they relied on manual tools. These tools were well adapted to the mountainous terrain and to the limited area of the terraces, called andenes, on which they often farmed.

politics.text: The Incas of Cusco began as one of the small ethnic groups, but expansion accelerated around the middle of the fifteenth century under the emperor Pachacuti. He ruled from a magnificently rebuilt Cusco, where he held absolute temporal and spiritual authority as the God of the Sun.

The Incas of Cusco began as one of the small and relatively minor Quechua ethnic groups. As early as the thirteenth century they began to absorb their neighbors, and conquest sped up around the middle of the fifteenth century under Pachacuti. He also issued a comprehensive code of laws and ruled as the God of the Sun from a rebuilt Cusco.

The Inca Empire was officially called the Realm of the Four Parts, or Tawantinsuyu in Quechua. Its administrative, political and military center was the city of Cusco. From 1438 to 1533 it grew into the largest empire in pre-Columbian America.

From 1438 to 1533, the Incas incorporated a large portion of western South America centered on the Andes, through conquest and peaceful assimilation, among other methods. Most peoples accepted Inca rule as a fait accompli and submitted peacefully, but refusal to accept it resulted in military conquest, and after a conquest the local rulers were executed. At its largest the empire joined modern-day Peru with parts of Ecuador, Bolivia, Argentina, Colombia and Chile.

The Incas of Cusco began as one of the small and relatively minor ethnic groups, the Quechuas. As early as the thirteenth century they began to expand and incorporate their neighbors. Expansion stayed slow until about the middle of the fifteenth century, when the pace of conquest began to accelerate.
Under the emperor Pachacuti and his son Topa Inca Yupanqui, the Incas came to control most of the Andean region. Their rule covered a population of 9 to 16 million inhabitants.

The Chimu were a loose confederation of walled cities scattered along the coast of northern Peru. They flourished from about 1140 to 1450, and their capital was Chan Chan outside of modern-day Trujillo. The source calls them the great city builders of pre-Inca civilization.

The Incas built their civilization through imperialistic militarism as well as careful and meticulous governmental management. Their government sponsored the construction of aqueducts and roads in addition to pre-existing installations. Some of these constructions still exist today.

The Inca ruler Viracocha Inca, born Hatun Tupaq Inca, took his name from the creator deity after seeing visions of the god in Urcos. He was the eighth Sapa Inka of the Kingdom of Cuzco and ruled from around 1410 to 1438.

Pachacuti promulgated a comprehensive code of laws to govern his far-flung empire. At the same time he consolidated his absolute temporal and spiritual authority as the God of the Sun. He ruled from a magnificently rebuilt Cusco.

The Inca Empire was preceded by two large-scale Andean empires, the Tiwanaku around Lake Titicaca and the Wari near Ayacucho. The Wari occupied the Cuzco area for about 400 years. Many Inca characteristics therefore derived from earlier multi-ethnic and expansive Andean cultures.
The Andes take their name most probably from the Quechua word anti, meaning east, as in Antisuyu, the east region. Antisuyu was one of the four regions of the Inca Empire.

Inca economic life rested on the ayllu, the basic unit of socio-territorial organisation. Officials took a census of the male population to decide whether labor conscription was needed, and individuals, adolescents included, were obligated to work on a revolving basis. Each resident was forced to give the Inca rulers a time of labor and a portion of their crops, and Inca officials received two-thirds of a farmer's crops. After local needs were satisfied, the state gathered the surplus from the ayllus and allocated it where it was needed, and populations of local chiefdoms received clothes, food, health care and schooling in exchange for their labour.

Inca farmers were not taxed on their production. Instead they had to work the lands of the emperor and the state religion for designated periods. Land was divided in roughly equal shares for the emperor, the state religion and the farmers themselves.

This part of the Rímac valley was administered by a local lord named Taulichusco, a former servant of Mama Vilo, one of the wives of Emperor Huayna Capac. His residential palace was located where the modern Palacio de Gobierno of Peru stands today. Nearby stood the temple-oracle of Rímac, one of the valley's main places of worship.

The Inca state was not the utopia Europeans imagined, according to the historian María Rostworowski. It depended on enormous quantities of accumulated goods to meet the constant demand for gifts required by reciprocity. Those gifts went to ethnic lords, military chiefs and the huacas, so a system of state storehouses was built.

philosophy.text: Viracocha was the creator and supreme deity of Inca mythology. He was believed to have made the universe, the sun, moon and stars, time itself and civilization. For the Inca, his cult was more important than the sun cult, and Inti came immediately after him.

The Inca divided their lands into four parts, and the empire's own name, Tawantinsuyu, means "four parts together." Cusco sat at the center, where the four sections met at Qorikancha, the temple of the sun. From there, ritual pathways led out across the empire.

The Incas built their religion by absorbing older Andean beliefs, most notably those of the Wari, Chavín and Nazca cultures. By combining these ancestral traditions, they created a highly centralized religious framework. It regulated almost every aspect of civic and spiritual life in the empire.

At Huanchaco, archaeologists excavated the bodies of 227 children and adolescents aged between four and 14, killed and buried between 1400 and 1450. Their sternums bore deep slashes and their rib cages were broken, indicating that their hearts may have been removed. Over 200 llama skeletons were also found. It is described as the largest-ever known example of child sacrifice.

Viracocha wandered the earth disguised as a beggar, teaching his creations the basics of civilization and working numerous miracles. Many refused to follow his teachings and devolved into warfare and delinquency, and he wept when he saw the plight of the creatures he had created. He eventually vanished across the Pacific Ocean by walking on the water, and never returned. It was thought that he would re-appear in times of trouble.

The Inca ruler was considered the living representative of the sun god Inti. Worship of Inti is regarded as an exploitation of religion for political purposes, because the Inca king was increasingly identified with the sun god.

According to one myth, Inti taught the founding Inca ancestor Manco Cápac and his daughter Mama Ocllo the arts of civilization. Inti then ordered his children to build the Inca capital where a divine golden bar they carried penetrated the earth. The Incas believed this happened at Cusco.

The Pleiades, called Qollqa, were honored as the mother of all the other stellar deities. When the constellation appeared after not being visible for 37 days, the start of the agricultural year was marked.

The ceque system was made up of 41 or 42 known pathways radiating out from the Qorikancha, the sun temple in Cusco. They led to huacas, shrines of religious and ceremonial significance. Some huacas were natural features such as springs, boulders or caves, while others were buildings, fountains or canals.

Anthropologist Haagen Klaus speculates that the Chimú might have turned to children when the sacrifice of adults was not enough to stop torrential rain and flooding caused by El Niño. At Huanchaco the children had deep slashes across the sternum and broken rib cages, indicating that their hearts may have been removed. If the analysis is correct, this was a mass killing of children in a religious response to a natural disaster.

R. Tom Zuidema theorized that the 328 huacas of the ceque system may each represent one day of a year measured as 12 circuits of the Moon. He also proposed that some of the lines served as astronomical sight lines, linking Inca ritual to their lunar calendar.

culture.text: The Chiribaya culture lived along about 220 kilometres of the Pacific coast of southern Peru and adjacent Chile. Its people had maritime settlements on the shore and farming settlements inland in river valleys. The classic phase of the culture ran from 1000 CE until 1360 CE.

The Chachapoyas, called the "Warriors of the Clouds," lived in the cloud forests of what is now northern Peru. Their culture began around the year 800 and lasted until the Inca conquest in about 1470. Much of what is known about them comes from ruins, pottery, tombs and other artifacts.

The Chiribaya lived in the Atacama Desert, where Ilo receives only 2.5 mm of rain a year. Farming was possible only where river or spring water could irrigate the land. Meanwhile the cold Humboldt Current offshore gave them one of the world's richest marine ecosystems.

Chan Chan, the capital of the Chimú kingdom of Chimor, was a large adobe city in the Moche Valley near present-day Trujillo. The Inca ruler Topa Inca Yupanqui led a campaign that conquered the Chimú around 1470 CE.

Centuries of drought weakened the Wari, and the city of Wari was dramatically depopulated by 1000 AD, though a small number of descendant groups still occupied it. Doorways in Wari and other government centers were deliberately blocked up, as if the Wari meant to return when the rains came back. The dwindling residents ceased all major construction. Archaeological evidence shows significant levels of interpersonal violence, suggesting that warfare and raiding increased among rival groups after the Wari state collapsed.

Before the Inca occupation of the area in the 15th century, a famous oracle in the Rímac Valley was known to visitors as Limaq, meaning "talker" or "speaker" in coastal Quechua. The Spanish eventually destroyed the oracle and replaced it with a church, but the name persisted.

About 1360 CE an uncharacteristic flood, probably caused by the El Niño Southern Oscillation, destroyed irrigation systems and many settlements in the Osmore valley. The area was depopulated. Many of the irrigation works were not repaired until Spanish colonists arrived in the late 16th century.

The Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de León noted that the Chachapoyas adopted customs imposed by the Cusco-based Inca after being annexed to the empire. The Inca conquest was not smooth: when the Chachapoyas rebelled under Huayna Capac, they killed all his governors and ministers along with a great number of soldiers and took others into slavery. After the Inca defeat of the Chachapoyas, large numbers were forced to resettle in remote parts of the empire. Because the Incas and conquistadors were the main sources of information, little first-hand knowledge of the Chachapoyas survives.

Genetic studies suggest the Chiribaya of the lower Osmore River Valley were likely descended in part from Wari and Tiwanaku colonists. The Chiribaya of the Azapa Valley in Chile were more likely descended from the ancient Chinchorro culture. This suggests the highland cultures had little direct contact with the Azapa Valley.
